blogs.title: Beyond Biphasic: Making Sense of Biphasic, Multiphasic, and Refractory Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Use this case of four discrete relapses after clarithromycin to clarify definitions and bedside distinctions between biphasic, multiphasic, sustained, and refractory anaphylaxis. We’ll walk through practical clues that suggest ongoing absorption vs true recurrence, how those labels change monitoring and treatment decisions, and how to document the course to guide future care.

blogs.title: Dose Matters: Why 0.5 mg IM Epinephrine Should Be Standard in Adults
blogs.description: This post dissects epinephrine dosing in adults ≥50 kg, highlighting the gap between guideline-recommended 0.5 mg IM and the ubiquitous 0.3 mg auto-injector. We’ll review pharmacology, emerging outcomes data showing more escalation when 0.3 mg is used first, strategies to operationalize 0.5 mg dosing in the ED/ICU, and how to balance speed (auto-injectors) with dose accuracy.

blogs.title: Watchful Waiting or Wires and Walls? Risk‑Stratified Observation After Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Observation after clinical resolution is still a gray zone. Using this multiphasic case, we compare traditional 4–6 hour observation with newer tiered strategies, discuss predictors that might warrant prolonged monitoring (severity, delayed epinephrine, multiple doses), and propose practical disposition frameworks for ED, step-down, and ICU, including when telemetry adds value.

blogs.title: Steroids in Anaphylaxis: Time to Step Away
blogs.description: Corticosteroids were given after the first relapse in this case, mirroring persistent real-world practice. We synthesize current evidence showing no reduction in biphasic events and possible harm, explain why steroids likely miss the relevant pathophysiology, and outline a steroid-sparing algorithm focused on timely epinephrine, supportive care, and clear discharge planning.

blogs.title: Getting the Tryptase Right: Sampling Windows, Interpretation, and the Mastocytosis Connection
blogs.description: The case underscores missed early tryptase sampling and later discovery of probable systemic mastocytosis. We review the optimal sampling schedule, the 1.2 × baseline + 2 rule to confirm mast cell activation, what to do when the first sample is late, and a practical approach to screening for clonal mast cell disease after severe or recurrent anaphylaxis.

blogs.title: When to Start an Epinephrine Infusion in Relapsing Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Repeated IM epinephrine worked here as symptoms attenuated, but the team debated an IV epinephrine infusion. This post outlines triggers to switch from intermittent IM to titrated infusion (hemodynamic instability, frequent redosing, airway involvement), suggested starting doses and monitoring, infusion pitfalls, and how to integrate fluids, antihistamines for skin-only symptoms, and escalation/de‑escalation plans.
